p: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.

notes: The article names the Ottoman commander İsa Bey (Evrenosoğlu) throughout, but once 'Ishak Bey Evrenoz'; I did not name him again (the description has him).

Casualties: the lead says 'killing and capturing up to 30,000 men'; the body says the dead 'may have been as high as 30,000, but it is unlikely that they suffered more than 15,000 deaths', plus 15,000 prisoners. I followed the body.
The article says Svetigrad and Berat were 'lost in 1448 and 1450 respectively'; left the years out.
Left out the burial of the Albanian dead at Shëmri and the first name Albulena for length.
